o: Assign each item to bag 1, bag 2, or neither, respecting capacities w1 and w2, maximizing total packed weight. Example 1 packs 5 + 4 = 9; Example 2 packs 8 + (3+4) = 15; Example 3 packs nothing. Sizes are tiny (n ≤ 100, capacities ≤ 300), so a 2-D knapsack dp[a][b] = best total with bag usages a and b is the intended solution — about 100·301·301 ≈ 9·10⁶ states.
k: State dp[a][b]: maximum weight using exactly/at-most a capacity in bag 1 and b in bag 2.
Each item has three choices, giving transitions from dp[a−x][b], dp[a][b−x], and dp[a][b].
Iterate items outer and capacities descending so each item is used at most once.

a.i: Process items one by one updating dp[a][b] in place with descending capacity loops (0/1 semantics). The final dp[w1][w2] is the answer.
s: For each weight x, for a from w1 down to 0, for b from w2 down to 0: dp[a][b] = max(dp[a][b], dp[a−x][b]+x if a≥x, dp[a][b−x]+x if b≥x).
a.t: O(n · w1 · w2) ≈ 9·10⁶ — triple nested loop over items and capacities.
a.sp: O(w1 · w2) for the dp table.

a.i: Same recurrence expressed recursively: f(i, a, b) = best packing of items i.. using remaining capacities a, b, with memoization on (i, a, b). Easier to derive in an interview; identical complexity.
s: f(i, a, b) = 0 when i = n.
Otherwise take max of skipping, bag 1 (if a ≥ x: x + f(i+1, a−x, b)), bag 2 (if b ≥ x: x + f(i+1, a, b−x)).
Memoize and return f(0, w1, w2).
a.t: O(n · w1 · w2) — each memoized state computed once with O(1) work.
a.sp: O(n · w1 · w2) for the memo table.

w: Bottom-up is preferred (no recursion depth concerns, less memory). Items may be skipped entirely — the dp naturally handles that; don't force assignment. Edge cases: no item fits (answer 0), duplicate weights. Follow-up: three bags, or minimize leftover capacity instead.
